tagline: Verbose, predictable, and everywhere in placements.
intro: Java is the safe default for Indian placement drives: nearly every online assessment platform supports it, the standard library is deep, and the JVM is fast enough that a clean O(n log n) solution never times out. The cost is ceremony — you will type more than in Python. Learn the Collections framework properly and most of that verbosity turns into muscle memory.

sections.title: Setup & Program Skeleton
sections.body_md: Install a JDK (21 LTS is a good default) and check `java -version`. Since JDK 11 you can run a single file directly with `java Main.java` — no separate `javac` step — which is ideal for practice. Online judges expect the class to be named `Main` and the file to match. Everything lives inside a class; there are no free functions.

sections.title: Fast Input / Output
sections.body_md: `Scanner` is convenient and far too slow: it does regex parsing per token and will time out past roughly 10^5 values. Use `BufferedReader` with `StringTokenizer` for input, and buffer your output too — `System.out.println` in a tight loop flushes constantly and is a common cause of a mysterious TLE.

sections.title: Types, Variables & Operators
sections.body_md: `int` is 32-bit and overflows silently at about 2.1 billion — no exception, just a wrong answer. Use `long` the moment sums or products could exceed that. Integer division truncates. `char` is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, and `char` arithmetic works, which is why `c - 'a'` is the standard way to index an alphabet array.

sections.title: Control Flow
sections.body_md: Standard C-family syntax. The enhanced `for` (`for (int x : arr)`) is cleaner when you don't need the index. Labelled `break` lets you exit nested loops in one step, which is genuinely useful in grid problems. Modern `switch` expressions remove the fall-through footgun.

sections.title: Methods, References & Scope
sections.body_md: Java is always pass-by-value — but for objects the value passed is the reference. So a method can mutate the array or list you hand it, yet cannot make your variable point at a different object. This distinction explains most surprises about "why did my array change?" and "why didn't my swap work?".

sections.title: Arrays & 2-D Arrays
sections.body_md: Arrays are fixed-length objects with a `.length` field (not a method). They are zero-initialised: `0`, `false`, or `null`. A 2-D array is an array of row references, so rows can differ in length — and copying a 2-D array with `clone()` copies only the row references, not the rows themselves.

sections.title: Strings
sections.body_md: `String` is immutable, so every concatenation allocates a new object — building a string with `+=` in a loop is O(n^2) and is the single most common performance mistake in Java interview code. Use `StringBuilder`. Compare with `.equals()`, never `==`: `==` compares references, and it appears to work for short literals because of the string pool, which makes the bug intermittent.

sections.title: The Collections Framework
sections.body_md: Java's answer to the STL. Declare variables by the interface (`List`, `Map`, `Set`, `Deque`) and instantiate the implementation — it keeps your code flexible and reads better in interviews. Collections hold objects, not primitives, so `List<Integer>` autoboxes; that costs memory and time, and it means `==` between two `Integer` objects can be false.

sections.title: Sorting & Comparators
sections.body_md: `Arrays.sort` on primitives is a dual-pivot quicksort with no stability guarantee and an O(n^2) adversarial worst case; on objects it is a stable merge sort. If worst-case matters on primitive input, box to `Integer[]`. `Comparator` has fluent factory methods that read far better than a hand-written `compare`, and `comparingInt` avoids boxing.

sections.title: Common Gotchas
sections.body_md: The bugs that cost real interview time: silent `int` overflow, `==` on strings and boxed integers, `+=` string building, and `NullPointerException` from a map lookup that returned `null` and was then unboxed. Also remember arrays print as a hash unless you use `Arrays.toString`, and that removing from a list while iterating throws `ConcurrentModificationException`.
